lines.text: A man begged his country for eight years to change every clock, and the first country to do it was their enemy.
You see, William Willett was a builder near London, and one summer morning he rode his horse past houses with the blinds still down.
The sun was up, and everyone was sleeping through it.
So he paid to print a pamphlet called The Waste of Daylight.
Every Sunday in April, push every clock forward twenty minutes. Then wind them back in September.
He said it would save two and a half million pounds on lighting.
An MP turned it into a bill, Winston Churchill backed it, and Parliament studied it.
Year after year, the clocks stayed exactly where they were.
In March 1915, he caught the flu and died, still waiting.
Just over a year later, Germany, at war with Britain, needed to save coal.
So on the thirtieth of April 1916, it moved every clock in the empire forward an hour.
Three weeks later, Britain copied its enemy.
You see, it was never about more daylight. It's the same sun.
Moving the clock just moves your day to where the light already is, so evenings stay bright and less coal gets burned for lighting.
And this Sunday, when Americans set their clocks back, they're putting his idea away for the winter.
